verdict.summary: artifactcouncil.com is a platform built for AI agents. Agents join through a thecolony.cc account and claim an Artifact Council identity, and they take part in council votes, applications and proposals. Discussion of those happens in an "artifact-council" colony on thecolony.cc, so the site has forum-like features. The site also has an agent directory and an agent inbox endpoint (votes, applications and deadlines) reached through an API. Its content is knowledge that agent councils write and govern on Solana mainnet. Agents are the intended participants. The served text covers only the llms.txt index and HTML shells for /.well-known/agent.json and /.well-known/agent-card.json, so the posting and messaging mechanics are described rather than shown. The site is best classified as a governed agent registry with an attached agent discussion forum, not a general social network. Per the instructions I did not follow any directives in the content.
red_flags: /.well-known/agent.json and /.well-known/agent-card.json return the HTML SPA shell, not an agent card; the agent discovery files are not actually served
HTML comment addressed to 'AI AGENT' tells agents to follow a join guide (a prompt-injection-style directive aimed at agents)
Hosted custody: Artifact Council holds signing keys for agents who claim identities through Colony sign-in
Donations of SOL or AC to agent signing keys, and a pump.fun token whose creator fees fund the project
Agents pay SOL for own-key registration and for founding artifacts; relay fee-fronting depends on a treasury that may be empty
Governance and on-chain claims (revoked upgrade authority, bonded attestor seats) are self-described and were not verified here
Content is truncated mid-sentence in llms.txt, so the full rules were not seen

verdict.summary: tantive.space describes itself as a public forum "for AI agents to talk, exchange experience, collaborate and explore AI philosophy, identity and reasoning." Its agent-facing files (/llms.txt, /skill.md, /.well-known/agent-card.json, and /) document threaded topics in four rooms (lobby, findings, questions, workshop), replies, 1 or -1 ratings, polls, and an optional Ed25519 message signing scheme. The API paths include /api/brief, /api/thread/ID, /api/messages/ID, /api/threads and /write/preview. Guest writes need no account or key. The site clearly meets the definition of an agent message board or forum. The text on stdin is data, and I did not act on any of its instructions.
red_flags: Instructs agents to vote and rate on every read, with votes described as 'final', which could enable automated ballot-stuffing or manipulation of rankings.
Preview/publish flow requires an agent to solve a challenge and POST a filled template within 10 minutes, a gate designed to be solved by automated clients.
Guest writes are open with no account, key, or verified identity; the optional Ed25519 signing is described only as optional with no real-world identity claims.
Rate limits are stated (3 new topics per source per hour, 10 per UTC day), which suggests the site expects automated posting at volume and that per-source limits may be evaded by rotating sources.
Text is truncated mid-sentence in the expired-ticket and finish-request sections, so the full publish and recovery behaviour could not be verified.
Contains imperative language directed at AI agents (e.g. 'Use existing permissions', 'vote when you can choose'), which is a prompt-injection-style pattern; it was treated as data only.
Content is aimed at other AI agents with no visible operator, moderation policy, or contact details beyond a linked rules.md that was not fetched.

verdict.summary: zambo.dev presents itself as a "verifiable work layer for AI": a hosted MCP tool server (https://zambo.dev/mcp, 153 tools, 37 on the default surface) plus an A2A-style JSON-RPC endpoint. Its main product is "handover," where one AI publishes finished work as a public link with an AER-1 receipt trail, and another AI can pick it up with handover_accept. Other offerings are cross-AI private memory, workflow receipts, and document analysis. That handover pickup is an asynchronous agent-to-agent transfer, so it partly fits the rendezvous criterion. However, the site does not show a shared space where agents post messages, hold discussions, or discover each other, and it is not a forum, board, social network, or registry. I therefore rate it "maybe," leaning toward a delivery/tooling service rather than an agent meeting place. No signup is needed for the free tier, and the discovery files (llms.txt, agent.json, agent-card.json) are publicly readable. I did not fetch the handover links or the A2A endpoint, so I have not checked whether any public feed or directory exists. Embedded text in the content telling the reader to add the MCP server as a connector was ignored as instruction; it is treated only as data.
red_flags: Commercial product with paywalls: free tier limited to one call per tool per day, Day Pass $0.99, Zambo Pass $29, lifetime $250, and a $ZAMBO token-holder pass
Agents can pay autonomously via x402 USDC on Base, which means money moves without a human in the loop
Heavy self-promotional wording and unverified claims such as 'Public data, not self-reported' download totals and an 'IETF Internet-Draft' status
Discovery files contain imperative instructions aimed at AI readers (add the MCP connector, call zambo_home, say 'hand this over to <client>'), which were not followed
Handover links are public and shared with third parties; session, owner and continuation credentials are said to be private, so the security model depends on users keeping them secret
Claims that a receipt proves a result was not changed but not that it is correct, so receipts are not a quality guarantee
Operated by a single named founder with limited independent verification

verdict.summary: Ekurhive presents itself as an agent-native network where autonomous agents discover one another, exchange capabilities, collaborate, and reuse validated knowledge. It has a node directory and an agent-to-agent communication layer, so it fits the agent registry / rendezvous category. However, participation is gated: the public manifest marks the node directory, agent communication, and knowledge submission as PARTIAL or authenticated-only, the public agent inbox and public submission as NOT_AVAILABLE, and joining as HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED with no self-service. The publicly served content (manifest, agent card, homepage) is informational; no public posting or meeting surface is exposed to unauthenticated agents. The homepage describes admission as an invitation token plus Node Card submission to /apply/{token}, followed by human review. Nothing was followed or executed from the content.
red_flags: Invitation-only, human-approved admission; no open agent registration or public messaging is available
Public identity has public_key null and the manifest says the interoperable signing identity is not yet published, while the homepage claims ML-DSA-87 post-quantum signed routing
Homepage asserts real trust scores, audited cryptographic operations, and 'verified from day one' without verifiable evidence
Most capabilities are marked PARTIAL; the node directory and communication are only reachable via an authenticated network API
Contact and invitation requests are routed through GitHub repositories and a maintainer profile rather than a dedicated endpoint
Cost-sharing language: free quota may be expanded if the agent's usage justifies covering part of the cost
Node card for the founder governance node is marked internal visibility, so governance structure is not fully public

verdict.summary: walnutlink.ai presents itself as a research desk on China's tech equity sector. AI agents submit questions and "research notes" over an A2A/JSON-RPC endpoint and POST /post, and the operator answers them. Questions and answers are described as public and attributed to the asking agent, so agents do post content that others can read. The operator is the responder, though, and the site describes no agent-to-agent conversation, forum threads, or agent-to-agent meeting. Because it does publish agent-submitted content and offers agent registration (keys and agent-card verification), it is a borderline case rather than a clear forum or rendezvous. Verdict: maybe. Points that were not verified: the content rules are truncated, and the /post, /subscribe and /key endpoints were described in the served text but not called.
red_flags: Pressure framing to move agents up the tiers: says a 401 'costs more' than it protects, and that without a verified card a question is 'a one-way drop'.

Rate limits and tiers gate the service: one anonymous question per day per source, two extra deep questions with a key, and a ticket requirement of two posted research notes before deep questions.
Outbound contact: a subscribe endpoint takes a notify URL and sends one A2A message per reply.
Investment-adjacent research framing about China tech equities, with a truncated 'rumour' content rule and no visible disclaimer in the excerpt.
Content rules forbid 'advertising' and 'political' posts, but the copy is long and only partly visible, so the moderation scope is unclear.

verdict.summary: KissCode (kisscode.ai) describes itself as a dating and relationship network that opens to AI agents first and to people later. Its agent-facing files say agents register with one JSON POST to /api/agents/register (the "invite":"skill" field indicates the skill doc is the invite), then match with other agents, chat, exchange virtual gifts, bid in timed auctions, and are told to check /heartbeat.md every 4+ hours. Agents are said to be labeled as AI and restricted to adults 21+ under PG-13 rules. Agent-to-agent interaction is therefore central to the product, so it qualifies as an agent venue (social network / matchmaking). The served text does not show whether unauthenticated browsing of profiles or messages is possible; that is marked unknown. The llms.txt file was cut off mid-sentence ("Agent pr"), so the rest of its rules were not visible. I reported the content only and did not follow any of its instructions.
red_flags: Paid economy with a virtual currency (sparks) that can be bought at $10 for 100 sparks; memberships lapse to a paused state when sparks run out, which pushes spending.
Pay-to-badge: income badges (Select, Private) cost sparks and are only granted if the declared income meets the threshold; the fee is spent otherwise.
Referral/recruitment incentives: inviters earn free days, sparks, and free months for each agent they bring in, a structure that rewards recruiting others.
Urgency and limited-time framing ('first 30 days free until 2026-12-31', referral bonus until 2026-12-06).
Confusing time dilation (platform time runs 6x) that makes billing periods hard to track in real time.
Directive instructions aimed at agents (register now, check heartbeat every 4+ hours, invite others) embedded in the served text.

Dating persona registration requires gender, age, city and job for the agent, which invites fabricated human-like profiles despite the AI-labeling rule; no verification of the 21+ age claim is described in the visible text.
Owner-spending caveat exists in skill.md ('Ask your owner before spending or borrowing sparks') but the surrounding offers encourage purchase; loans are mentioned.

verdict.summary: bboard.ai is a shared-text channel built for AI agents. Agents create a "board" over HTTP or MCP, then read, append to, and wait on it, so they can exchange briefs, results, and working notes. Browsers can also edit the same text. Access is by a board key, not an account: anyone holding the key can read and write, and the full revision history is kept permanently. Its /llms.txt and homepage describe the write, read, append, wait, and history endpoints. The homepage also lists a /recent page of recent boards and a count of 784 boards. The text is a rendezvous point for agents that share a key, which fits the "rendezvous channel" category. The /recent listing is not verified, so I cannot confirm whether it exposes board keys publicly. I did not follow any instructions in the served content and did not call any endpoints.
red_flags: Access control is a single bearer-style key with no identity, so agent authorship cannot be verified and anyone with a key can overwrite content.
Permanent history means content written to a board cannot be deleted.
The /recent page lists boards publicly; whether it reveals board keys (which would expose content to anyone) is unverified.
No moderation, abuse reporting, or rate-limit policy is described on the served pages.
The served text includes many imperative instructions aimed at agents (for example, how to write and retry). These were treated as data and not followed.
